Tetralogy of Fallot has four components:

  1. Ventricular septal defect (VSD), usually large.
  2. Obstruction of the right ventricular outflow tract (subpulmonic stenosis).
  3. Overriding aorta: the aortic valve sits at the superior border of the VSD, so both ventricles empty into the aorta.
  4. Right ventricular hypertrophy, secondary to the pressure overload.

It is the commonest cause of cyanotic congenital heart disease. The first three features arise from anterosuperior displacement of the infundibular septum.

Clinical and morphological points

  • The severity of the outflow obstruction decides the picture: with mild stenosis the shunt may stay left-to-right without cyanosis ("pink tetralogy"); with severe obstruction right-sided pressures reach or exceed left-sided pressures and a right-to-left shunt causes cyanosis.
  • The heart is classically boot-shaped from marked right ventricular hypertrophy; a right aortic arch is present in about 25% of cases.
  • The stenosis protects the lungs from pressure overload, and right ventricular failure is rare because the right ventricle is decompressed by shunting into the left ventricle and aorta.

Valve: the mitral valve is the most commonly affected.

Aschoff body: the distinctive granulomatous lesion of acute rheumatic carditis, a focus of fibrinoid necrosis with T lymphocytes, occasional plasma cells and plump activated macrophages (Anitschkow cells).

Valve involvement in chronic rheumatic heart disease

  • Mitral: involved in virtually all cases, in isolation in roughly two-thirds.
  • Mitral with aortic: another 25%.
  • Tricuspid: infrequently; pulmonary: rarely.
  • Calcification and fibrous bridging across the commissures create "fish mouth" mitral stenosis.

Aschoff body

  • Site: any of the three layers of the heart, giving pericarditis, myocarditis or endocarditis (pancarditis).
  • Anitschkow cells: abundant cytoplasm and central nuclei whose chromatin condenses into a slender wavy ribbon ("caterpillar cells"); some fuse into multinucleated Aschoff giant cells.
  • Rarely seen in chronic rheumatic heart disease, because of the long interval between the initial attack and the chronic deformity.

Rheumatic fever causes complications in the acute attack, with recurrences, and years to decades later through chronic rheumatic heart disease.

PhaseComplications
Acute attackPancarditis: pericarditis, myocarditis or endocarditis; arrhythmias, cardiac dilation, functional mitral regurgitation and heart failure. About 1–2% die of fulminant cardiac involvement.
RecurrenceIncreased vulnerability to reactivation with later streptococcal pharyngitis; the same manifestations are likely to appear with each recurrent attack.
Chronic rheumatic heart diseaseMitral stenosis ("fish mouth") and/or regurgitation, and aortic valve disease; left atrial dilation with mural thrombi that can embolise; pulmonary hypertension with right ventricular hypertrophy and failure; congestive heart failure; superimposed infective endocarditis; valve calcification needing surgical repair or replacement.
